stars.label: Proof
stars.title: Proof
stars.body: A proof is a chain of steps where each one is forced by the ones before it. The Greeks made it the heart of mathematics, and Euclid’s Elements shows it at work: a few plain starting points and a long tower built on them.

stars.label: Axioms
stars.title: Axioms
stars.body: Every proof starts somewhere. Axioms are the statements accepted without proof, such as Euclid’s postulates about points and lines, or Peano’s rules for the counting numbers. Choosing them is a quiet act that everything after depends on.

stars.label: Infinity
stars.title: Infinity
stars.body: Cantor showed that infinities come in different sizes. The counting numbers can be listed one after another, and the real numbers cannot. His diagonal argument builds a number that differs from the n-th entry of any list in its n-th digit. A close cousin of that move sits inside Gödel’s proof.

stars.label: Zero
stars.title: Zero
stars.body: Zero began as an empty place in a written number and slowly became a number of its own. Indian mathematicians, among them Brahmagupta in the seventh century, wrote down rules for calculating with it. From there it travelled with the numerals into the Arab world and Europe. verify

stars.label: Computation
stars.title: Computation
stars.body: In 1936 Turing described a machine that follows simple rules and asked what such machines can decide. The halting problem, whether a program will ever stop, has no general answer. It is the same kind of limit Gödel found, seen from the side of programs.

stars.label: Symmetry
stars.title: Symmetry
stars.body: A symmetry is a change that leaves something looking the same. Group theory turned that into an exact language, and Galois used it to explain why some equations can be solved by formulas and others cannot. Noether later tied symmetries of physical laws to quantities that stay constant, like energy.

stars.label: Prime numbers
stars.title: Prime numbers
stars.body: Primes are the numbers that cannot be split into smaller factors, and every whole number is built from them in exactly one way. Euclid showed there are infinitely many. Gödel used them as letters when he turned statements into numbers.

stars.label: Geometry
stars.title: Geometry
stars.body: Geometry began as measuring land and became the study of shape and space. For two thousand years people tried to derive Euclid’s fifth postulate from the others. In the nineteenth century it turned out that it cannot be derived, and other consistent geometries exist.

stars.label: Number and proportion
stars.title: Number and proportion
stars.body: Comparing sizes by ratio is one of the oldest mathematical habits. The Pythagoreans found it in the lengths of plucked strings, and later it became fractions, scale and the idea that some quantities, like the diagonal of a square, have no ratio at all.

stars.label: Algorithms
stars.title: Algorithms
stars.body: An algorithm is a recipe exact enough for a machine to follow. The word comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, who wrote in Baghdad in the ninth century on calculating with the Indian numerals and on solving equations.

stars.label: Models of the world
stars.title: Models of the world
stars.body: Mathematics keeps turning out to describe things it was not built for. Orbits follow ellipses, waves follow sums of sines, and populations follow growth curves. Why that works so well is an old question and still an open one.

sources.t: Wikipedia: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences

stars.label: Math
stars.title: Math
stars.body: A way into mathematics through what it is built on and where it reaches: proof, axioms and infinity at the base, symmetry and number as its patterns, and the places where it meets computers and the physical world. Gödel sits at the foundations.

stars.label: Clocks
stars.title: Clocks
stars.body: From shadows on a sundial to water clocks, pendulums and quartz, clocks are anything that repeats steadily. Since 1967 the second has been defined by the vibration of caesium atoms, which makes the best clocks agree to within a second over many millions of years.

stars.label: Day, month, year
stars.title: Day, month, year
stars.body: The sky offers three clocks: the turning of the Earth, the phases of the Moon and the cycle of seasons. They do not fit evenly into each other, a year is about 365.24 days and a lunar month about 29.5, and the long work of making them agree is the story of calendars.

stars.label: Calendars
stars.title: Calendars
stars.body: A calendar is an agreement about how to count days against the sky. Some follow the Moon, some the Sun, many try to follow both, and each needs small repairs: leap days, leap months, skipped dates. Behind every one sits astronomy, arithmetic and a community that wants to meet on the same day.

stars.label: Time as a cycle
stars.title: Time as a cycle
stars.body: Many traditions see time as something that returns. The Maya combined a 260-day count with a 365-day year, which meet again every 52 years, and wrote longer counts on top. A line and a circle both live inside most calendars. verify

stars.label: The arrow of time
stars.title: The arrow of time
stars.body: Most basic laws of physics work the same running forward or backward. Yet eggs break and do not unbreak. The usual answer is entropy: there are far more disordered arrangements than ordered ones, and the early universe began in an unusually ordered state.

stars.label: Time and motion
stars.title: Time and motion
stars.body: In relativity, two clocks need not agree. A clock on a fast journey runs slow, and a clock higher in a gravitational field runs a little faster than one lower down. Satellite navigation has to correct for both effects to stay accurate.

stars.label: Gödel’s rotating universe
stars.title: Gödel’s rotating universe
stars.body: In 1949 Gödel found a solution of Einstein’s equations for a universe that turns as a whole and contains paths that return to their own past. It showed that general relativity alone does not forbid such loops, and he took this as a hint that time may not be what it seems.

stars.label: The felt present
stars.title: The felt present
stars.body: The present we feel has some width. William James called it the specious present, a short stretch of a few seconds in which we hear a phrase of music or a spoken sentence as one thing. It is where memory, expectation and attention meet.

stars.label: Memory and the past
stars.title: Memory and the past
stars.body: Remembering is a way of rebuilding a past moment each time, and it can shift in the retelling. Cultures keep a shared past in songs, stories and written records, and that is where time meets history.

stars.label: Time
stars.title: Time
stars.body: A way into time through how it is measured, how physics treats it and how it is felt and told. The sky gave the first clocks, music gives time its rhythm, and Gödel asked in his own way what time is.

stars.label: The naked-eye sky
stars.title: The naked-eye sky
stars.body: Before telescopes, people learned the sky by patient watching: the Sun’s path, the Moon’s phases, the wandering planets against the fixed stars. Those records set the calendars, the seasons for planting and the first predictions.

stars.label: Light takes time
stars.title: Light takes time
stars.body: Light travels fast and still takes time. Sunlight is about eight minutes old when it reaches us, and the light of the Andromeda galaxy has travelled around two and a half million years. Looking farther away is looking further back.

stars.label: Telescopes
stars.title: Telescopes
stars.body: In 1609 and 1610 Galileo pointed a telescope at the sky and saw mountains on the Moon, phases of Venus and four moons circling Jupiter. Each new kind of telescope since, from radio dishes to space observatories, has opened another kind of sky.

stars.label: Orbits
stars.title: Orbits
stars.body: Kepler found that planets move on ellipses and that a line from the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times. Newton later showed that one law of gravity explains all of it. For a while Kepler also hoped to find music in the planetary distances.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Kepler’s laws of planetary motion

stars.label: Lives of stars
stars.title: Lives of stars
stars.body: Stars form in clouds of gas, shine by fusing light elements into heavier ones, and end in a way set mostly by their mass: as a white dwarf, a neutron star or a black hole. Most of the carbon, oxygen and iron around us was made inside earlier stars.

stars.label: The expanding universe
stars.title: The expanding universe
stars.body: In the 1920s Lemaître and Hubble found that distant galaxies move away from us, and the farther they are the faster they go. The simplest reading is that space itself is stretching, and that the universe was once much smaller and hotter.

stars.label: The cosmic web
stars.title: The cosmic web
stars.body: On the largest scales galaxies are not scattered evenly. They gather along filaments and sheets around huge empty voids, like a web. Gravity grew this pattern from tiny differences in the early universe.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Large-scale structure of the universe

stars.label: Constellations
stars.title: Constellations
stars.body: A constellation is a pattern people draw between stars, and the patterns differ between cultures. The familiar Western figures come mostly from Greek and Mesopotamian sources, while other traditions read the sky differently, for instance the dark shapes in the dust lanes of the Milky Way that Andean peoples named. verify

stars.label: Archaeoastronomy
stars.title: Archaeoastronomy
stars.body: Archaeoastronomy studies how people of the past watched and used the sky: alignments of buildings to the Sun or stars, calendars, and the stories told about what happens above. It sits where astronomy meets archaeology, anthropology and history.

stars.label: Cosmovisions
stars.title: Cosmovisions
stars.body: A cosmovision is a way of seeing the cosmos that holds knowledge, practice and meaning together. Many Indigenous traditions understand the sky as part of the same world as land, people and time, and this invites a conversation with astronomy that goes in both directions.

stars.label: Astronomy
stars.title: Astronomy
stars.body: A way into astronomy through how we look, what we found about the large structure of things, and how people in different places read the same sky. It connects to time through the calendar and to history through the records kept by watchers.

stars.label: Writing
stars.title: Writing
stars.body: Writing appeared in Mesopotamia more than five thousand years ago, and an early use was keeping accounts of grain and goods. Over time it came to hold laws, letters, poems and calculations, and it lets one person speak to someone far away in place and time.

stars.label: Oral traditions
stars.title: Oral traditions
stars.body: Many peoples keep their past in song, story and ritual. Memory is helped by rhythm, repetition and place, and a long chain of tellers can carry knowledge across many generations.

stars.label: Records of the sky
stars.title: Records of the sky
stars.body: The Babylonian astronomical diaries record the Moon, planets, weather and eclipses night after night over several centuries. The sky was one of the first things people wrote down systematically, and those records are still used today.

stars.label: How numbers travelled
stars.title: How numbers travelled
stars.body: Our digits came from India, passed through the Arab world and reached Europe in the Middle Ages, helped by books such as Fibonacci’s Liber Abaci of 1202. With them came the place-value system and zero, which made written arithmetic far easier than with Roman numerals.

stars.label: Translation and the House of Wisdom
stars.title: Translation and the House of Wisdom
stars.body: In ninth-century Baghdad, scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic and added their own. Algebra and much of astronomy were carried and extended there before returning to Europe in translation. verify

stars.label: Routes and exchange
stars.title: Routes and exchange
stars.body: Ideas travel along the same roads as goods. The Silk Roads, sea lanes and river valleys carried spices, paper, numbers and stories, and many discoveries belong to the meeting of peoples.

stars.label: Sources and voices
stars.title: Sources and voices
stars.body: Every account is written by someone, for someone, at some moment. Historians ask who wrote it, who is missing, and what survived by chance. A past told only from the records of the powerful has gaps that other sources, including oral ones, can help fill.

stars.label: Dating the past
stars.title: Dating the past
stars.body: Tree rings, layers in ice and radiocarbon in old wood and bone give dates to things without calendars. Eclipses in old chronicles act as anchor points, because astronomers can compute exactly when each one happened.

stars.label: History
stars.title: History
stars.body: A way into history through how the past is kept, how ideas and numbers moved between peoples, and how we come to know what happened. Writing, memory and the sky are three of its oldest records.
